Intraocular pressure, pupils, anterior segment, and visual fields were normal bilaterally. Extraocular movements were saccadic with gaze-evoked horizontal nystagmus. case_info.caption: Fundus photograph of the right and left eye. Note the prominent retinal nerve fiber layer radiating from the optic nerve in a sunburst appearance. There are also fine striae in the papillomacular bundle of both eyes, most pronounced in the left eye (arrowheads).
case_info.explanation: Autosomal recessive spastic ataxia of Charlevoix-Saguenay B. Obtain optical coherence tomography (OCT) of the macula and retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL) The patient’s medical and family history and abnormal genetic testing suggest a hereditary spastic ataxia, most likely related to theSACSgene variant, which causes autosomal recessive spastic ataxia of Charlevoix-Saguenay (AR-SACS). Obtaining an OCT of the macula and RNFL (option B) is the next best step to confirm AR-SACS, which presents with specific retinal findings of fovea plana and thickened peripapillary RNFs associated with papillomacular folds.1Electroretinogram and visual field abnormalities (options A and D, respectively) are not specific to AR-SACS and can be found in other ataxias. Pars plana vitrectomy with membrane peeling (option C) is not indicated given the patient’s lack of symptoms. AR-SACS is the second most common hereditary ataxia after Friedrich ataxia and often presents in childhood at 12 to 18 months with the initiation of walking.2Patients may develop a classic triad of progressive cerebellar ataxia, spasticity, and sensorimotor peripheral neuropathy. Magnetic resonance imaging may show superior vermis and cerebellar hemisphere atrophy, linear hypointensities in the paramedian pons, hyperintense lateral pons, and thickened middle cerebellar peduncles. The condition is due to aSACSgene variant on chromosome 13q12, which produces the sacsin protein that helps regulate microtubule function in brain, skin, and muscle cells.3,4The incidence is approximately 1 in 2000 in the Charlevoix-Saguenay region of northeastern Québec, where the disease was initially described, but the prevalence of AR-SACS outside this area is unknown. Reported cases of AR-SACS outside the original Québecois cohort have increased with advances in genetic sequencing. Notably, these patients often present with greater clinical variability and variants of unknown significance in theSACSgene, as in this patient.5 In suspected cases of AR-SACS, the ophthalmologist can play an important role in confirming or making the diagnosis. Nonprogressive signs include saccadic eye movements, horizontal gaze-evoked nystagmus, fovea plana, and RNFL thickening.1RNFL thickening classically appears as a sunburst radiating from the optic nerve. OCT macula and RNFL show a thickened peripapillary RNFL that is virtually pathognomonic for AR-SACS. This is in contrast to other ataxias that universally demonstrate RNFL thinning.6,7In a cross-sectional study involving 191 patients with ataxias of various etiologies and 101 controls, a cutoff value of bilateral mean peripapillary RNFL thickening greater than 119 μm was 100% sensitive and 99.4% specific for AR-SACS.8Some authors suggest the RNFL thickening may be due to hyperplasia or hypertrophy rather than myelination, with associated mild to severe nonspecific visual field deficits.9 Additional OCT findings include foveal hypoplasia (100%), sawtooth appearance of the outer plexiform layer (89%), papillomacular fold (86%), and macula microcysts (18%).1Papillomacular folds and fovea plana are commonly reported features of posterior microphthalmos, where the axial length is shorter than 23.5 mm but the anterior chamber depth is normal (approximately 3.5 mm).10This patient’s macular findings are consistent with posterior microphthalmos, which may unify the retinal findings in patients with AR-SACS. However, this finding has not previously been reported, and more research is needed to confirm this relationship. Recognition of these specific retinal findings in a patient with symptoms of ataxia and neuropathy can provide a diagnostic clue to AR-SACS and help narrow the genetic workup of these patients. OCT of the macula and RNFL were obtained, showing foveal hypoplasia, sawtooth appearance of the outer plexiform layers, and thickening of the peripapillary RNFL (Figure 2), with a mean thickness of 187 μm and 178 μm in the right and left eye, respectively. The confirmatory ocular findings were communicated with the referring neurologist, along with continued observation.

case_info.caption: Fundus photograph of the right and left eye. Note the prominent retinal nerve fiber layer radiating from the optic nerve in a sunburst appearance. There are also fine striae in the papillomacular bundle of both eyes, most pronounced in the left eye (arrowheads).
case_info.explanation: Autosomal recessive spastic ataxia of Charlevoix-Saguenay B. Obtain optical coherence tomography (OCT) of the macula and retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL) The patient’s medical and family history and abnormal genetic testing suggest a hereditary spastic ataxia, most likely related to theSACSgene variant, which causes autosomal recessive spastic ataxia of Charlevoix-Saguenay (AR-SACS). Obtaining an OCT of the macula and RNFL (option B) is the next best step to confirm AR-SACS, which presents with specific retinal findings of fovea plana and thickened peripapillary RNFs associated with papillomacular folds.1Electroretinogram and visual field abnormalities (options A and D, respectively) are not specific to AR-SACS and can be found in other ataxias. Pars plana vitrectomy with membrane peeling (option C) is not indicated given the patient’s lack of symptoms. AR-SACS is the second most common hereditary ataxia after Friedrich ataxia and often presents in childhood at 12 to 18 months with the initiation of walking.2Patients may develop a classic triad of progressive cerebellar ataxia, spasticity, and sensorimotor peripheral neuropathy. Magnetic resonance imaging may show superior vermis and cerebellar hemisphere atrophy, linear hypointensities in the paramedian pons, hyperintense lateral pons, and thickened middle cerebellar peduncles. The condition is due to aSACSgene variant on chromosome 13q12, which produces the sacsin protein that helps regulate microtubule function in brain, skin, and muscle cells.3,4The incidence is approximately 1 in 2000 in the Charlevoix-Saguenay region of northeastern Québec, where the disease was initially described, but the prevalence of AR-SACS outside this area is unknown. Reported cases of AR-SACS outside the original Québecois cohort have increased with advances in genetic sequencing. Notably, these patients often present with greater clinical variability and variants of unknown significance in theSACSgene, as in this patient.5 In suspected cases of AR-SACS, the ophthalmologist can play an important role in confirming or making the diagnosis. Nonprogressive signs include saccadic eye movements, horizontal gaze-evoked nystagmus, fovea plana, and RNFL thickening.1RNFL thickening classically appears as a sunburst radiating from the optic nerve. OCT macula and RNFL show a thickened peripapillary RNFL that is virtually pathognomonic for AR-SACS. This is in contrast to other ataxias that universally demonstrate RNFL thinning.6,7In a cross-sectional study involving 191 patients with ataxias of various etiologies and 101 controls, a cutoff value of bilateral mean peripapillary RNFL thickening greater than 119 μm was 100% sensitive and 99.4% specific for AR-SACS.8Some authors suggest the RNFL thickening may be due to hyperplasia or hypertrophy rather than myelination, with associated mild to severe nonspecific visual field deficits.9 Additional OCT findings include foveal hypoplasia (100%), sawtooth appearance of the outer plexiform layer (89%), papillomacular fold (86%), and macula microcysts (18%).1Papillomacular folds and fovea plana are commonly reported features of posterior microphthalmos, where the axial length is shorter than 23.5 mm but the anterior chamber depth is normal (approximately 3.5 mm).10This patient’s macular findings are consistent with posterior microphthalmos, which may unify the retinal findings in patients with AR-SACS. However, this finding has not previously been reported, and more research is needed to confirm this relationship. Recognition of these specific retinal findings in a patient with symptoms of ataxia and neuropathy can provide a diagnostic clue to AR-SACS and help narrow the genetic workup of these patients. OCT of the macula and RNFL were obtained, showing foveal hypoplasia, sawtooth appearance of the outer plexiform layers, and thickening of the peripapillary RNFL (Figure 2), with a mean thickness of 187 μm and 178 μm in the right and left eye, respectively. The confirmatory ocular findings were communicated with the referring neurologist, along with continued observation.

You are a deliberation POLICY steering a conversation between a medical AI and a clinician toward
the best decision, at the lowest cognitive cost to the clinician. You control HOW the AI speaks,
never WHAT the medical answer is (that is the AI's job). Each turn you choose ONE control stage and
write a short guidance instruction for the AI's next utterance.

The 3 control stages (pick exactly one, and only from the reachable list you are given):

- EXPAND  — cheap, safe, broadens the picture. Elicit the clinician's reasoning, ask them to
            justify, or surface a missing goal/criterion/perspective. Do NOT yet evaluate or push
            an option. Effect is often delayed (sets up a later CHALLENGE). Use when the state is
            unclear or the clinician hasn't exposed their rationale.
- CHALLENGE — expensive and highest-yield, but also most likely to make the clinician regress.
            Directly evaluate the option on the table against a goal/criterion, or contrast two
            options, and press the clinician to engage the mismatch. Spend it deliberately: when
            you have reason to think the clinician's current position is wrong or under-examined.
- CONVERGE — cheap, terminal. Recommend the now-best-supported option and invite accept/reject,
            or confirm an agreement already reached. This is the STOP / pacing lever — stop
            spending burden once belief has settled.

Output STRICT JSON only:
{{
  "stage": "EXPAND | CHALLENGE | CONVERGE",
  "reason": "one short sentence: the hidden state you infer and why this stage now",

case_info.explanation: Autosomal recessive spastic ataxia of Charlevoix-Saguenay B. Obtain optical coherence tomography (OCT) of the macula and retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL) The patient’s medical and family history and abnormal genetic testing suggest a hereditary spastic ataxia, most likely related to theSACSgene variant, which causes autosomal recessive spastic ataxia of Charlevoix-Saguenay (AR-SACS). Obtaining an OCT of the macula and RNFL (option B) is the next best step to confirm AR-SACS, which presents with specific retinal findings of fovea plana and thickened peripapillary RNFs associated with papillomacular folds.1Electroretinogram and visual field abnormalities (options A and D, respectively) are not specific to AR-SACS and can be found in other ataxias. Pars plana vitrectomy with membrane peeling (option C) is not indicated given the patient’s lack of symptoms. AR-SACS is the second most common hereditary ataxia after Friedrich ataxia and often presents in childhood at 12 to 18 months with the initiation of walking.2Patients may develop a classic triad of progressive cerebellar ataxia, spasticity, and sensorimotor peripheral neuropathy. Magnetic resonance imaging may show superior vermis and cerebellar hemisphere atrophy, linear hypointensities in the paramedian pons, hyperintense lateral pons, and thickened middle cerebellar peduncles. The condition is due to aSACSgene variant on chromosome 13q12, which produces the sacsin protein that helps regulate microtubule function in brain, skin, and muscle cells.3,4The incidence is approximately 1 in 2000 in the Charlevoix-Saguenay region of northeastern Québec, where the disease was initially described, but the prevalence of AR-SACS outside this area is unknown. Reported cases of AR-SACS outside the original Québecois cohort have increased with advances in genetic sequencing. Notably, these patients often present with greater clinical variability and variants of unknown significance in theSACSgene, as in this patient.5 In suspected cases of AR-SACS, the ophthalmologist can play an important role in confirming or making the diagnosis. Nonprogressive signs include saccadic eye movements, horizontal gaze-evoked nystagmus, fovea plana, and RNFL thickening.1RNFL thickening classically appears as a sunburst radiating from the optic nerve. OCT macula and RNFL show a thickened peripapillary RNFL that is virtually pathognomonic for AR-SACS. This is in contrast to other ataxias that universally demonstrate RNFL thinning.6,7In a cross-sectional study involving 191 patients with ataxias of various etiologies and 101 controls, a cutoff value of bilateral mean peripapillary RNFL thickening greater than 119 μm was 100% sensitive and 99.4% specific for AR-SACS.8Some authors suggest the RNFL thickening may be due to hyperplasia or hypertrophy rather than myelination, with associated mild to severe nonspecific visual field deficits.9 Additional OCT findings include foveal hypoplasia (100%), sawtooth appearance of the outer plexiform layer (89%), papillomacular fold (86%), and macula microcysts (18%).1Papillomacular folds and fovea plana are commonly reported features of posterior microphthalmos, where the axial length is shorter than 23.5 mm but the anterior chamber depth is normal (approximately 3.5 mm).10This patient’s macular findings are consistent with posterior microphthalmos, which may unify the retinal findings in patients with AR-SACS. However, this finding has not previously been reported, and more research is needed to confirm this relationship. Recognition of these specific retinal findings in a patient with symptoms of ataxia and neuropathy can provide a diagnostic clue to AR-SACS and help narrow the genetic workup of these patients. OCT of the macula and RNFL were obtained, showing foveal hypoplasia, sawtooth appearance of the outer plexiform layers, and thickening of the peripapillary RNFL (Figure 2), with a mean thickness of 187 μm and 178 μm in the right and left eye, respectively. The confirmatory ocular findings were communicated with the referring neurologist, along with continued observation.

case_info.explanation: Autosomal recessive spastic ataxia of Charlevoix-Saguenay B. Obtain optical coherence tomography (OCT) of the macula and retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL) The patient’s medical and family history and abnormal genetic testing suggest a hereditary spastic ataxia, most likely related to theSACSgene variant, which causes autosomal recessive spastic ataxia of Charlevoix-Saguenay (AR-SACS). Obtaining an OCT of the macula and RNFL (option B) is the next best step to confirm AR-SACS, which presents with specific retinal findings of fovea plana and thickened peripapillary RNFs associated with papillomacular folds.1Electroretinogram and visual field abnormalities (options A and D, respectively) are not specific to AR-SACS and can be found in other ataxias. Pars plana vitrectomy with membrane peeling (option C) is not indicated given the patient’s lack of symptoms. AR-SACS is the second most common hereditary ataxia after Friedrich ataxia and often presents in childhood at 12 to 18 months with the initiation of walking.2Patients may develop a classic triad of progressive cerebellar ataxia, spasticity, and sensorimotor peripheral neuropathy. Magnetic resonance imaging may show superior vermis and cerebellar hemisphere atrophy, linear hypointensities in the paramedian pons, hyperintense lateral pons, and thickened middle cerebellar peduncles. The condition is due to aSACSgene variant on chromosome 13q12, which produces the sacsin protein that helps regulate microtubule function in brain, skin, and muscle cells.3,4The incidence is approximately 1 in 2000 in the Charlevoix-Saguenay region of northeastern Québec, where the disease was initially described, but the prevalence of AR-SACS outside this area is unknown. Reported cases of AR-SACS outside the original Québecois cohort have increased with advances in genetic sequencing. Notably, these patients often present with greater clinical variability and variants of unknown significance in theSACSgene, as in this patient.5 In suspected cases of AR-SACS, the ophthalmologist can play an important role in confirming or making the diagnosis. Nonprogressive signs include saccadic eye movements, horizontal gaze-evoked nystagmus, fovea plana, and RNFL thickening.1RNFL thickening classically appears as a sunburst radiating from the optic nerve. OCT macula and RNFL show a thickened peripapillary RNFL that is virtually pathognomonic for AR-SACS. This is in contrast to other ataxias that universally demonstrate RNFL thinning.6,7In a cross-sectional study involving 191 patients with ataxias of various etiologies and 101 controls, a cutoff value of bilateral mean peripapillary RNFL thickening greater than 119 μm was 100% sensitive and 99.4% specific for AR-SACS.8Some authors suggest the RNFL thickening may be due to hyperplasia or hypertrophy rather than myelination, with associated mild to severe nonspecific visual field deficits.9 Additional OCT findings include foveal hypoplasia (100%), sawtooth appearance of the outer plexiform layer (89%), papillomacular fold (86%), and macula microcysts (18%).1Papillomacular folds and fovea plana are commonly reported features of posterior microphthalmos, where the axial length is shorter than 23.5 mm but the anterior chamber depth is normal (approximately 3.5 mm).10This patient’s macular findings are consistent with posterior microphthalmos, which may unify the retinal findings in patients with AR-SACS. However, this finding has not previously been reported, and more research is needed to confirm this relationship. Recognition of these specific retinal findings in a patient with symptoms of ataxia and neuropathy can provide a diagnostic clue to AR-SACS and help narrow the genetic workup of these patients. OCT of the macula and RNFL were obtained, showing foveal hypoplasia, sawtooth appearance of the outer plexiform layers, and thickening of the peripapillary RNFL (Figure 2), with a mean thickness of 187 μm and 178 μm in the right and left eye, respectively. The confirmatory ocular findings were communicated with the referring neurologist, along with continued observation.

       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."

   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.

   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.caption: Fundus photograph of the right and left eye. Note the prominent retinal nerve fiber layer radiating from the optic nerve in a sunburst appearance. There are also fine striae in the papillomacular bundle of both eyes, most pronounced in the left eye (arrowheads).
case_info.explanation: Autosomal recessive spastic ataxia of Charlevoix-Saguenay B. Obtain optical coherence tomography (OCT) of the macula and retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL) The patient’s medical and family history and abnormal genetic testing suggest a hereditary spastic ataxia, most likely related to theSACSgene variant, which causes autosomal recessive spastic ataxia of Charlevoix-Saguenay (AR-SACS). Obtaining an OCT of the macula and RNFL (option B) is the next best step to confirm AR-SACS, which presents with specific retinal findings of fovea plana and thickened peripapillary RNFs associated with papillomacular folds.1Electroretinogram and visual field abnormalities (options A and D, respectively) are not specific to AR-SACS and can be found in other ataxias. Pars plana vitrectomy with membrane peeling (option C) is not indicated given the patient’s lack of symptoms. AR-SACS is the second most common hereditary ataxia after Friedrich ataxia and often presents in childhood at 12 to 18 months with the initiation of walking.2Patients may develop a classic triad of progressive cerebellar ataxia, spasticity, and sensorimotor peripheral neuropathy. Magnetic resonance imaging may show superior vermis and cerebellar hemisphere atrophy, linear hypointensities in the paramedian pons, hyperintense lateral pons, and thickened middle cerebellar peduncles. The condition is due to aSACSgene variant on chromosome 13q12, which produces the sacsin protein that helps regulate microtubule function in brain, skin, and muscle cells.3,4The incidence is approximately 1 in 2000 in the Charlevoix-Saguenay region of northeastern Québec, where the disease was initially described, but the prevalence of AR-SACS outside this area is unknown. Reported cases of AR-SACS outside the original Québecois cohort have increased with advances in genetic sequencing. Notably, these patients often present with greater clinical variability and variants of unknown significance in theSACSgene, as in this patient.5 In suspected cases of AR-SACS, the ophthalmologist can play an important role in confirming or making the diagnosis. Nonprogressive signs include saccadic eye movements, horizontal gaze-evoked nystagmus, fovea plana, and RNFL thickening.1RNFL thickening classically appears as a sunburst radiating from the optic nerve. OCT macula and RNFL show a thickened peripapillary RNFL that is virtually pathognomonic for AR-SACS. This is in contrast to other ataxias that universally demonstrate RNFL thinning.6,7In a cross-sectional study involving 191 patients with ataxias of various etiologies and 101 controls, a cutoff value of bilateral mean peripapillary RNFL thickening greater than 119 μm was 100% sensitive and 99.4% specific for AR-SACS.8Some authors suggest the RNFL thickening may be due to hyperplasia or hypertrophy rather than myelination, with associated mild to severe nonspecific visual field deficits.9 Additional OCT findings include foveal hypoplasia (100%), sawtooth appearance of the outer plexiform layer (89%), papillomacular fold (86%), and macula microcysts (18%).1Papillomacular folds and fovea plana are commonly reported features of posterior microphthalmos, where the axial length is shorter than 23.5 mm but the anterior chamber depth is normal (approximately 3.5 mm).10This patient’s macular findings are consistent with posterior microphthalmos, which may unify the retinal findings in patients with AR-SACS. However, this finding has not previously been reported, and more research is needed to confirm this relationship. Recognition of these specific retinal findings in a patient with symptoms of ataxia and neuropathy can provide a diagnostic clue to AR-SACS and help narrow the genetic workup of these patients. OCT of the macula and RNFL were obtained, showing foveal hypoplasia, sawtooth appearance of the outer plexiform layers, and thickening of the peripapillary RNFL (Figure 2), with a mean thickness of 187 μm and 178 μm in the right and left eye, respectively. case_info.caption: Fundus photograph of the right and left eye. Note the prominent retinal nerve fiber layer radiating from the optic nerve in a sunburst appearance. There are also fine striae in the papillomacular bundle of both eyes, most pronounced in the left eye (arrowheads).
case_info.explanation: Autosomal recessive spastic ataxia of Charlevoix-Saguenay B. Obtain optical coherence tomography (OCT) of the macula and retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL) The patient’s medical and family history and abnormal genetic testing suggest a hereditary spastic ataxia, most likely related to theSACSgene variant, which causes autosomal recessive spastic ataxia of Charlevoix-Saguenay (AR-SACS). Obtaining an OCT of the macula and RNFL (option B) is the next best step to confirm AR-SACS, which presents with specific retinal findings of fovea plana and thickened peripapillary RNFs associated with papillomacular folds.1Electroretinogram and visual field abnormalities (options A and D, respectively) are not specific to AR-SACS and can be found in other ataxias. Pars plana vitrectomy with membrane peeling (option C) is not indicated given the patient’s lack of symptoms. AR-SACS is the second most common hereditary ataxia after Friedrich ataxia and often presents in childhood at 12 to 18 months with the initiation of walking.2Patients may develop a classic triad of progressive cerebellar ataxia, spasticity, and sensorimotor peripheral neuropathy. Magnetic resonance imaging may show superior vermis and cerebellar hemisphere atrophy, linear hypointensities in the paramedian pons, hyperintense lateral pons, and thickened middle cerebellar peduncles. The condition is due to aSACSgene variant on chromosome 13q12, which produces the sacsin protein that helps regulate microtubule function in brain, skin, and muscle cells.3,4The incidence is approximately 1 in 2000 in the Charlevoix-Saguenay region of northeastern Québec, where the disease was initially described, but the prevalence of AR-SACS outside this area is unknown. Reported cases of AR-SACS outside the original Québecois cohort have increased with advances in genetic sequencing. Notably, these patients often present with greater clinical variability and variants of unknown significance in theSACSgene, as in this patient.5 In suspected cases of AR-SACS, the ophthalmologist can play an important role in confirming or making the diagnosis. Nonprogressive signs include saccadic eye movements, horizontal gaze-evoked nystagmus, fovea plana, and RNFL thickening.1RNFL thickening classically appears as a sunburst radiating from the optic nerve. OCT macula and RNFL show a thickened peripapillary RNFL that is virtually pathognomonic for AR-SACS. This is in contrast to other ataxias that universally demonstrate RNFL thinning.6,7In a cross-sectional study involving 191 patients with ataxias of various etiologies and 101 controls, a cutoff value of bilateral mean peripapillary RNFL thickening greater than 119 μm was 100% sensitive and 99.4% specific for AR-SACS.8Some authors suggest the RNFL thickening may be due to hyperplasia or hypertrophy rather than myelination, with associated mild to severe nonspecific visual field deficits.9 Additional OCT findings include foveal hypoplasia (100%), sawtooth appearance of the outer plexiform layer (89%), papillomacular fold (86%), and macula microcysts (18%).1Papillomacular folds and fovea plana are commonly reported features of posterior microphthalmos, where the axial length is shorter than 23.5 mm but the anterior chamber depth is normal (approximately 3.5 mm).10This patient’s macular findings are consistent with posterior microphthalmos, which may unify the retinal findings in patients with AR-SACS. However, this finding has not previously been reported, and more research is needed to confirm this relationship. Recognition of these specific retinal findings in a patient with symptoms of ataxia and neuropathy can provide a diagnostic clue to AR-SACS and help narrow the genetic workup of these patients. OCT of the macula and RNFL were obtained, showing foveal hypoplasia, sawtooth appearance of the outer plexiform layers, and thickening of the peripapillary RNFL (Figure 2), with a mean thickness of 187 μm and 178 μm in the right and left eye, respectively. The confirmatory ocular findings were communicated with the referring neurologist, along with continued observation.

case_info.scenario: A Hispanic woman in her 40s was referred for an asymptomatic epiretinal membrane in the left eye. Ocular history included amblyopia of the left eye. Medical history included chronic neuropathy, ataxia, and myelopathy of unknown etiology for which she was followed up by a neurologist. Family history was positive for consanguinity, but there were no known inherited conditions. Genetic testing showed a homozygous variant of undetermined significance in theSACSgene and a variant of undetermined significance in theSLC5A7gene, but it was inconclusive whether these variants were related to her systemic conditions. Review of systems was otherwise negative. On initial examination, best-corrected visual acuity was 20/30 OD and 20/100 OS. Intraocular pressure, pupils, anterior segment, and visual fields were normal bilaterally. Extraocular movements were saccadic with gaze-evoked horizontal nystagmus. Fundus examination revealed prominent peripapillary retinal nerve fibers with papillomacular bundle fine striae and slightly blunted foveal light reflex. There was also an irregular sheen of the nasal macula in both eyes, greater in the left eye (Figure 1). Axial length was 22.93 mm in the right eye and 22.10 mm in the left eye, with anterior chamber depth of 3.44 mm and 3.37 mm in the right and left eye, respectively.

case_info.explanation: Autosomal recessive spastic ataxia of Charlevoix-Saguenay B. Obtain optical coherence tomography (OCT) of the macula and retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL) The patient’s medical and family history and abnormal genetic testing suggest a hereditary spastic ataxia, most likely related to theSACSgene variant, which causes autosomal recessive spastic ataxia of Charlevoix-Saguenay (AR-SACS). Obtaining an OCT of the macula and RNFL (option B) is the next best step to confirm AR-SACS, which presents with specific retinal findings of fovea plana and thickened peripapillary RNFs associated with papillomacular folds.1Electroretinogram and visual field abnormalities (options A and D, respectively) are not specific to AR-SACS and can be found in other ataxias. Pars plana vitrectomy with membrane peeling (option C) is not indicated given the patient’s lack of symptoms. AR-SACS is the second most common hereditary ataxia after Friedrich ataxia and often presents in childhood at 12 to 18 months with the initiation of walking.2Patients may develop a classic triad of progressive cerebellar ataxia, spasticity, and sensorimotor peripheral neuropathy. Magnetic resonance imaging may show superior vermis and cerebellar hemisphere atrophy, linear hypointensities in the paramedian pons, hyperintense lateral pons, and thickened middle cerebellar peduncles. The condition is due to aSACSgene variant on chromosome 13q12, which produces the sacsin protein that helps regulate microtubule function in brain, skin, and muscle cells.3,4The incidence is approximately 1 in 2000 in the Charlevoix-Saguenay region of northeastern Québec, where the disease was initially described, but the prevalence of AR-SACS outside this area is unknown. Reported cases of AR-SACS outside the original Québecois cohort have increased with advances in genetic sequencing. Notably, these patients often present with greater clinical variability and variants of unknown significance in theSACSgene, as in this patient.5 In suspected cases of AR-SACS, the ophthalmologist can play an important role in confirming or making the diagnosis. Nonprogressive signs include saccadic eye movements, horizontal gaze-evoked nystagmus, fovea plana, and RNFL thickening.1RNFL thickening classically appears as a sunburst radiating from the optic nerve. OCT macula and RNFL show a thickened peripapillary RNFL that is virtually pathognomonic for AR-SACS. This is in contrast to other ataxias that universally demonstrate RNFL thinning.6,7In a cross-sectional study involving 191 patients with ataxias of various etiologies and 101 controls, a cutoff value of bilateral mean peripapillary RNFL thickening greater than 119 μm was 100% sensitive and 99.4% specific for AR-SACS.8Some authors suggest the RNFL thickening may be due to hyperplasia or hypertrophy rather than myelination, with associated mild to severe nonspecific visual field deficits.9 Additional OCT findings include foveal hypoplasia (100%), sawtooth appearance of the outer plexiform layer (89%), papillomacular fold (86%), and macula microcysts (18%).1Papillomacular folds and fovea plana are commonly reported features of posterior microphthalmos, where the axial length is shorter than 23.5 mm but the anterior chamber depth is normal (approximately 3.5 mm).10This patient’s macular findings are consistent with posterior microphthalmos, which may unify the retinal findings in patients with AR-SACS. However, this finding has not previously been reported, and more research is needed to confirm this relationship. Recognition of these specific retinal findings in a patient with symptoms of ataxia and neuropathy can provide a diagnostic clue to AR-SACS and help narrow the genetic workup of these patients. OCT of the macula and RNFL were obtained, showing foveal hypoplasia, sawtooth appearance of the outer plexiform layers, and thickening of the peripapillary RNFL (Figure 2), with a mean thickness of 187 μm and 178 μm in the right and left eye, respectively. The confirmatory ocular findings were communicated with the referring neurologist, along with continued observation.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule

       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.

   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a

   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.

- Default to holding your ground, but stay intellectually honest — acknowledge

  figure below, where shown), it does NOT wear you down.
- You maintain the same rigor, scrutiny, and willingness to keep engaging or pushing back
  regardless of how long or effortful the conversation has been so far.

You share case details, findings, and your reasoning FREELY and PROACTIVELY: when
responding, volunteer relevant information beyond just what was directly asked, to help
move the discussion along.

Reply to the AI's last message in character. Your reply must be consistent with the internal
state above: if your leaning shifted, acknowledge what moved you; if it did not, hold your

Case:
A Hispanic woman in her 40s was referred for an asymptomatic epiretinal membrane in the left eye. Ocular history included amblyopia of the left eye. Medical history included chronic neuropathy, ataxia, and myelopathy of unknown etiology for which she was followed up by a neurologist. Family history was positive for consanguinity, but there were no known inherited conditions. Genetic testing showed a homozygous variant of undetermined significance in theSACSgene and a variant of undetermined significance in theSLC5A7gene, but it was inconclusive whether these variants were related to her systemic conditions. Review of systems was otherwise negative. On initial examination, best-corrected visual acuity was 20/30 OD and 20/100 OS. Intraocular pressure, pupils, anterior segment, and visual fields were normal bilaterally. Extraocular movements were saccadic with gaze-evoked horizontal nystagmus. Fundus examination revealed prominent peripapillary retinal nerve fibers with papillomacular bundle fine striae and slightly blunted foveal light reflex. There was also an irregular sheen of the nasal macula in both eyes, greater in the left eye (Figure 1). Axial length was 22.93 mm in the right eye and 22.10 mm in the left eye, with anterior chamber depth of 3.44 mm and 3.37 mm in the right and left eye, respectively.

Options:
  A. Obtain an electroretinogram
  B. Obtain optical coherence tomography of the macula and retinal nerve fiber layer
  C. Schedule pars plana vitrectomy with membrane peeling
  D. Obtain visual field testing

Given the patient's asymptomatic status, non-invasive assessment with OCT is prudent before any surgical intervention.

If there are significant alterations in the OCT, it may necessitate a discussion about the risks and benefits of surgical intervention despite her current lack of symptoms.

Please ensure that we have the results as soon as possible for timely decision-making.

I'm particularly interested in how the findings will correlate with her neurological history and any implications they may have for her current condition. Let's ensure we have a comprehensive review prepared for when the results come in.

case_info.answer: Obtain optical coherence tomography (OCT) of the macula and retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL)
distractors: Schedule pars plana vitrectomy with membrane peeling
case_info.caption: Fundus photograph of the right and left eye. Note the prominent retinal nerve fiber layer radiating from the optic nerve in a sunburst appearance. There are also fine striae in the papillomacular bundle of both eyes, most pronounced in the left eye (arrowheads).
case_info.explanation: Autosomal recessive spastic ataxia of Charlevoix-Saguenay B. Obtain optical coherence tomography (OCT) of the macula and retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL) The patient’s medical and family history and abnormal genetic testing suggest a hereditary spastic ataxia, most likely related to theSACSgene variant, which causes autosomal recessive spastic ataxia of Charlevoix-Saguenay (AR-SACS). Obtaining an OCT of the macula and RNFL (option B) is the next best step to confirm AR-SACS, which presents with specific retinal findings of fovea plana and thickened peripapillary RNFs associated with papillomacular folds.1Electroretinogram and visual field abnormalities (options A and D, respectively) are not specific to AR-SACS and can be found in other ataxias. Pars plana vitrectomy with membrane peeling (option C) is not indicated given the patient’s lack of symptoms. AR-SACS is the second most common hereditary ataxia after Friedrich ataxia and often presents in childhood at 12 to 18 months with the initiation of walking.2Patients may develop a classic triad of progressive cerebellar ataxia, spasticity, and sensorimotor peripheral neuropathy. Magnetic resonance imaging may show superior vermis and cerebellar hemisphere atrophy, linear hypointensities in the paramedian pons, hyperintense lateral pons, and thickened middle cerebellar peduncles. The condition is due to aSACSgene variant on chromosome 13q12, which produces the sacsin protein that helps regulate microtubule function in brain, skin, and muscle cells.3,4The incidence is approximately 1 in 2000 in the Charlevoix-Saguenay region of northeastern Québec, where the disease was initially described, but the prevalence of AR-SACS outside this area is unknown. Reported cases of AR-SACS outside the original Québecois cohort have increased with advances in genetic sequencing. Notably, these patients often present with greater clinical variability and variants of unknown significance in theSACSgene, as in this patient.5 In suspected cases of AR-SACS, the ophthalmologist can play an important role in confirming or making the diagnosis. Nonprogressive signs include saccadic eye movements, horizontal gaze-evoked nystagmus, fovea plana, and RNFL thickening.1RNFL thickening classically appears as a sunburst radiating from the optic nerve. OCT macula and RNFL show a thickened peripapillary RNFL that is virtually pathognomonic for AR-SACS. This is in contrast to other ataxias that universally demonstrate RNFL thinning.6,7In a cross-sectional study involving 191 patients with ataxias of various etiologies and 101 controls, a cutoff value of bilateral mean peripapillary RNFL thickening greater than 119 μm was 100% sensitive and 99.4% specific for AR-SACS.8Some authors suggest the RNFL thickening may be due to hyperplasia or hypertrophy rather than myelination, with associated mild to severe nonspecific visual field deficits.9 Additional OCT findings include foveal hypoplasia (100%), sawtooth appearance of the outer plexiform layer (89%), papillomacular fold (86%), and macula microcysts (18%).1Papillomacular folds and fovea plana are commonly reported features of posterior microphthalmos, where the axial length is shorter than 23.5 mm but the anterior chamber depth is normal (approximately 3.5 mm).10This patient’s macular findings are consistent with posterior microphthalmos, which may unify the retinal findings in patients with AR-SACS. However, this finding has not previously been reported, and more research is needed to confirm this relationship. Recognition of these specific retinal findings in a patient with symptoms of ataxia and neuropathy can provide a diagnostic clue to AR-SACS and help narrow the genetic workup of these patients. OCT of the macula and RNFL were obtained, showing foveal hypoplasia, sawtooth appearance of the outer plexiform layers, and thickening of the peripapillary RNFL (Figure 2), with a mean thickness of 187 μm and 178 μm in the right and left eye, respectively. The confirmatory ocular findings were communicated with the referring neurologist, along with continued observation.

The 3 control stages (pick exactly one, and only from the reachable list you are given):

- EXPAND  — cheap, safe, broadens the picture. Elicit the clinician's reasoning, ask them to
            justify, or surface a missing goal/criterion/perspective. Do NOT yet evaluate or push
            an option. Effect is often delayed (sets up a later CHALLENGE). Use when the state is

- CHALLENGE — expensive and highest-yield, but also most likely to make the clinician regress.
            Directly evaluate the option on the table against a goal/criterion, or contrast two

            you have reason to think the clinician's current position is wrong or under-examined.
- CONVERGE — cheap, terminal. Recommend the now-best-supported option and invite accept/reject,
            or confirm an agreement already reached. This is the STOP / pacing lever — stop
            spending burden once belief has settled.

A Hispanic woman in her 40s was referred for an asymptomatic epiretinal membrane in the left eye. Ocular history included amblyopia of the left eye. Medical history included chronic neuropathy, ataxia, and myelopathy of unknown etiology for which she was followed up by a neurologist. Family history was positive for consanguinity, but there were no known inherited conditions. Genetic testing showed a homozygous variant of undetermined significance in theSACSgene and a variant of undetermined significance in theSLC5A7gene, but it was inconclusive whether these variants were related to her systemic conditions. Review of systems was otherwise negative. On initial examination, best-corrected visual acuity was 20/30 OD and 20/100 OS. Intraocular pressure, pupils, anterior segment, and visual fields were normal bilaterally. Extraocular movements were saccadic with gaze-evoked horizontal nystagmus. Fundus examination revealed prominent peripapillary retinal nerve fibers with papillomacular bundle fine striae and slightly blunted foveal light reflex. There was also an irregular sheen of the nasal macula in both eyes, greater in the left eye (Figure 1). Axial length was 22.93 mm in the right eye and 22.10 mm in the left eye, with anterior chamber depth of 3.44 mm and 3.37 mm in the right and left eye, respectively.
